evidence: Col. 5.2.10: Estō hexagōnum quōquō versus līneīs pedum XXX
terms.comment: Greek ἑξάγωνον, in Columella’s chapter on measuring fields; Varro writes it in Greek letters (Varr. RR 3.16.5, Lewis & Short). Latin also says it plainly: sex angulōrum, “of six corners” (Columella, in the same place), and sexangulus.
The Latin adjective, used by Ovid and Pliny of the cells of a honeycomb.

phrases.latin: Numerā angulōs hujus cellae: sex sunt. Hexagōnum est, ut in favō.
phrases.english: Count the corners of this cell: there are six. It’s a hexagon, as in a honeycomb.

phrases.latin: nōn in favō sex angulīs cella, totidem quot habet ipsa pedēs?
phrases.english: doesn’t each cell in the honeycomb have six corners, as many as the bee herself has legs?

phrases.latin: Sī fuerit sex angulōrum, in quadrātōs pedēs sīc redigitur. Estō hexagōnum quōquō versus līneīs pedum XXX.
phrases.english: If it has six corners, it is reduced to square feet like this. Let there be a hexagon with sides of thirty feet each way.

sources: Lewis & Short: hexagonum · Lewis & Short: sexangulus
